sources.quote: My dear Young, The saltimbanques cannot come to Berneval so I don't know if there are enough attractions to drag you and Mrs Young out so long a way.
sources.context: Wilde to Dalhousie Young, [? 2 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Hyde). The saltimbanques are travelling acrobats. Wilde had been out of prison a fortnight and Young, who had defended him in print two years earlier while a stranger, was proposing to visit with his wife.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Young came to see him within a fortnight of his release.
sources.provenance: PDF page 925; printed folio 875 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: To sum up shortly: I do not see any evidence that Mr Wilde's love for beauty was a pose; and if there were such evidence it would not affect me in the least. His books do not seem to me to contain any element that is morbid or immoral. I can find no trace of bad influence in his friendships; and for the question of his life, as he was convicted (rightly or wrongly, it makes no difference) of breaking a law, he is being punished for breaking a law. As regards sin, even if we know, or think we know what a man has done, we know nothing about the motive or the manner; and under these circumstances, any outside judgment is a mere impertinence.
sources.context: The close of Young's pamphlet Apologia pro Oscar Wilde, dated 31 May 1895 - six days after the conviction - quoted in full by the editors. Young was A stranger to Wilde when he wrote it. The editors add that he also contributed £50 to the fund More Adey collected for Wilde's release. This is Young's own voice, not Wilde's, and is the reason the node exists.
sources.speaker: Dalhousie Young
sources.supports: A public defence of Wilde published by a stranger six days after the conviction.

name: Dalhousie Young
bio: English composer and pianist (1866-1921), a pupil of Leschetizky and Paderewski, who made his début in Rome in 1893 and in London in 1895. Within days of Wilde's conviction that spring - and while a complete stranger to him - he published a pamphlet, Apologia pro Oscar Wilde, dated 31 May 1895. He also gave £50 to the fund More Adey collected to support Wilde on his release. Seven of Wilde's letters to him survive, all from the Berneval summer of 1897.
